title: Are Notifications Actually Making Us Anxious?
metaTitle: Are Notifications Actually Making Us Anxious?
metaDescription: Notifications interrupt, leave attention residue, and feed anticipatory checking. The link to anxiety is plausible but mostly correlational. Here's the picture.
keyFinding: Notifications reliably fragment attention and feed anticipatory checking, and the pattern is plausibly linked to low-grade anxiety, but the strongest evidence is about interruption and attention cost rather than a proven direct cause of an anxiety disorder.
honestAnswer: Notifications clearly do something to attention, and there is reasonable evidence that constant interruption and the habit of anticipatory checking are associated with feeling more stressed and scattered. But "making us anxious" is a stronger claim than the data cleanly supports. Most of the well-established findings are about the cost of interruption and the pull of anticipated alerts, with the link to anxiety being plausible and partly correlational rather than a proven one-way cause.

The more defensible summary is that a steady stream of interruptions keeps attention fragmented and the nervous system in a mild state of readiness, and that this is uncomfortable for many people — while clinical anxiety has many causes and is not something notifications alone explain. The good news is that the interruption side of this is one of the more controllable parts of modern life.
whatDataShows: The clearest finding concerns interruption, not anxiety directly. Sophie Leroy's research on "attention residue" showed that when people switch from one task to another, part of their attention stays stuck on the previous task, degrading performance on the new one. A notification is an interruption that triggers exactly this: even a glance leaves residue, so the cost of an alert is not just the seconds spent reading it but the lingering drag on whatever you return to.

There is also the phenomenon of anticipatory or habitual checking — reaching for the phone in expectation of an alert, sometimes before any has arrived. A related, well-documented experience is the "phantom vibration," the sensation that your phone buzzed when it didn't; surveys of phone users have found a large majority report having felt it at least occasionally. It is generally read as a sign of how primed people become to detect and respond to alerts, rather than as a disorder in itself.

On the anxiety link specifically, the evidence is more mixed. Some experimental work suggests that batching notifications or going without them can reduce stress and improve mood and attention for some people, while other studies find effects that are small or depend heavily on the person and the type of alert. The honest reading is that constant interruption and constant availability are plausibly arousing and stressful, but the research base is largely correlational and the effect sizes are modest, so notifications are better described as one contributor to feeling on edge than as a proven cause of anxiety.
whyItFeelsDifferent: It feels like notifications barely cost anything because each one is tiny — a glance, a few seconds. What's hidden is the residue: the part of your attention that stays snagged on the interruption after you've put the phone down. The felt cost is one alert; the real cost is the fragmented attention that follows, which is much harder to notice from the inside.

Constant availability also feels normal because it arrived gradually, but it represents a genuine shift — for most of human history, you were not reachable by everyone at all times. Being persistently reachable keeps a low-level expectation running in the background that something may need your response, and that mild, sustained readiness is exactly the kind of arousal people often experience as a vague unease rather than as a clear cause they can name.

And anticipatory checking feels like your own free choice each time, which obscures how habitual it has become. The phantom vibration is the clearest tell that the habit has its own momentum: the impulse to check can fire even with no actual signal, because you've become finely tuned to detect one.
whatResearchSaysToDo: The intervention with the most consistent support is reducing interruptions rather than reducing the phone entirely: turning off non-essential notifications, batching the rest to set times, and using do-not-disturb during focused work. Because the documented cost is interruption and attention residue, fewer interruptions is the lever that most directly targets the mechanism.

Creating predictable check-in windows can reduce anticipatory checking, because much of the pull comes from not knowing whether something is waiting. When checking happens on a schedule you set rather than on every buzz, the background "is there something I need to see" tension has fewer openings to fire.

For the arousal side, ordinary nervous-system basics apply — and this page is educational only, not medical advice. If anxiety is persistent and affecting your daily life, the right step is a qualified clinician, not a notification setting. Managing alerts may make the day feel calmer, but it is not a treatment for an anxiety disorder, and treating it as one can delay help that works.
whatDoesNotHelp: Simply trying to ignore notifications while leaving them switched on tends not to work, because the cost is paid the moment your attention is pulled — even an alert you choose not to act on has already interrupted you and left residue. The decision to ignore comes after the interruption, not instead of it.

Assuming notifications are the sole cause of feeling anxious is also a mistake, and a potentially harmful one. Anxiety has many sources, and pinning it entirely on the phone can mean overlooking sleep, stress, health, or circumstances that matter more — and can delay seeking help that actually addresses it.

Going fully offline in dramatic, short bursts — a one-day cleanse followed by a return to the same settings — rarely produces lasting change, because it doesn't alter the steady stream of interruptions you come back to. The research favours changing the default settings over occasional total abstinence.
realNumbersInContext: There is no clean "notifications cause X% more anxiety" figure, and you should be wary of anyone who offers one. What is reasonably established is the interruption cost: switching tasks leaves attention residue, so the price of an alert extends well beyond the moment of reading it. Surveys on phantom vibrations have repeatedly found that a large majority of regular phone users — often reported in the range of two-thirds or more — have experienced the sensation of a buzz that never happened, which illustrates how primed people become to detect alerts.

On the wellbeing side, experimental studies that reduce or batch notifications have reported improvements in attention, productivity, and mood for some participants, but the effects are generally modest and vary by person. The fair conclusion is that interruption and constant availability plausibly raise low-grade arousal and stress, while the direct causal link to clinical anxiety remains uncertain — context that argues for managing notifications without over-claiming what doing so will fix.
keyTakeaways: The clearest, best-established cost of notifications is interruption and 'attention residue,' not a proven direct cause of anxiety.
Even a glance leaves residue: the real cost of an alert is the lingering drag on whatever you return to, not the seconds spent reading it.
The link to anxiety is plausible but largely correlational and modest — notifications are one contributor to feeling on edge, not a proven cause.
Reducing interruptions — turning off non-essential alerts, batching, do-not-disturb — targets the mechanism most directly.
This is educational context, not medical advice: persistent anxiety warrants a qualified clinician, not a notification setting.

But the cost was already paid the moment your attention was pulled — attention residue means part of your focus stays snagged on the interruption after you put the phone down. The decision to ignore comes after the interruption, not instead of it, which is why simply ignoring notifications while leaving them switched on tends not to work.

faqs.question: Do notifications actually cause anxiety?
faqs.answer: The honest answer is uncertain. Notifications reliably interrupt attention and feed anticipatory checking, and constant availability plausibly raises low-grade arousal — but the evidence linking them directly to clinical anxiety is largely correlational and modest. They're better described as one contributor to feeling on edge than as a proven cause.

faqs.question: What is 'attention residue'?
faqs.answer: It's Sophie Leroy's finding that when you switch tasks, part of your attention stays stuck on the previous one, hurting performance on the next. A notification triggers this even with a quick glance — so the real cost of an alert isn't the few seconds reading it, but the lingering drag on whatever you return to.

faqs.question: Why do I feel my phone buzz when it didn't?
faqs.answer: That's a 'phantom vibration,' and it's very common — surveys find a large majority of regular phone users have experienced it. It's generally read not as a disorder but as a sign of how primed people become to detect and respond to alerts when notifications are a constant part of the day.

faqs.question: Does turning off notifications help?
faqs.answer: For the interruption and attention side, it's the most directly supported step — turning off non-essential alerts, batching the rest, and using do-not-disturb during focused work targets the actual mechanism. Effects on mood are real but modest and vary by person, so it tends to make the day feel calmer rather than transform how you feel.

faqs.question: I feel anxious a lot. Is it my phone?
faqs.answer: Possibly a contributor, but anxiety has many causes and pinning it entirely on the phone risks overlooking sleep, stress, health, or circumstances that may matter more. This is educational only, not medical advice — if anxiety is persistent and affecting your life, a qualified clinician is the right step, not a notification setting.
